summary: Defines the application/tei+xml media type for markup languages defined under the Text Encoding Initiative guidelines, used to encode texts for scholarship. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A label stuck on a file saying it is a scholarly text marked up in a certain way, so programs know how to open it.

subtitle: Register a MIME type for scholarly text markup documents.

tldr.problem: Text Encoding and Interchange (TEI) is a widely used XML standard for scholarly and archival texts, but it lacked an official MIME media type to tell applications what they are receiving.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers the MIME type 'application/tei+xml' for TEI documents, following the XML media type conventions established in RFC 3023, so applications can recognize and process TEI files correctly.
tldr.outcome: TEI documents can now be served over HTTP and other protocols with proper content-type headers, enabling better interoperability among libraries, archives, publishers, and scholarly tools.

today: RFC 6129 is an Informational RFC that remains current. The registration of application/tei+xml as an official MIME type is still used in the scholarly and digital humanities communities for serving TEI documents over the Internet. The RFC supports the ongoing work of libraries, archives, and universities in digitizing and sharing cultural heritage materials.

sections.title: What is TEI?
sections.content:
Text Encoding and Interchange (TEI) is an international and interdisciplinary standard used by libraries, museums, publishers, and individual scholars to represent all kinds of textual material for online research and teaching. TEI documents are XML files that encode scholarly texts—everything from historical manuscripts to modern literature—with detailed markup describing structure, meaning, and editorial annotations.

This RFC registers an official MIME media type so that web servers, browsers, and applications can correctly identify and process TEI files when they are transmitted over the Internet using standard HTTP and other protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: TEI is a special way of marking up old books and manuscripts so computers can understand the structure and content. Programs need to know when they are receiving a TEI file.

sections.title: TEI Document Structure
sections.content:
TEI files are XML documents with a root element in the TEI namespace. The most common root elements are <TEI>, which contains a single document, and <teiCorpus>, which bundles multiple documents into one file. TEI documents typically consist of a teiHeader (metadata about the text) followed by a <text> element (the actual content).

Files are often given extensions such as .tei, .teiCorpus, or .odd (One Document Does it All, a special TEI file that includes schema fragments and documentation used for defining TEI variants). However, file extensions are not reliable for identification across the Internet, which is why a proper MIME type is necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: A TEI file is an XML document that starts with a header describing the text, then includes the actual marked-up content. Multiple texts can be bundled together in one file.

sections.title: Media Type Registration
sections.content:
The RFC registers the MIME media type application/tei+xml according to RFC 3023, the standard for XML-based media types. The media type requires no mandatory parameters, though it supports an optional charset parameter (typically UTF-8) matching the conventions of application/xml.

When a TEI document is transmitted over HTTP, the server should include the header Content-Type: application/tei+xml to inform the client what type of content is being received. This allows browsers and applications to route the document to the appropriate handler.
sections.plainLanguage: The official name for TEI files is 'application/tei+xml', like how JPEG images are labeled 'image/jpeg'. Programs can now look at this label to know how to handle the file.

sections.title: Security and Rights Considerations
sections.content:
TEI documents are often used for digitizing cultural heritage materials, which may have intellectual property, authenticity, or confidentiality concerns. Some historical documents may be legally binding centuries after they were written, requiring cryptographic technologies to assure their authenticity and integrity. Other materials may be confidential and require content filtering or encryption.

TEI provides fine-grained markup for attribution at the element level, allowing different parts of a document to have different ownership or restrictions. Applications processing TEI documents must respect this granular markup and honor intellectual property and Digital Rights Management constraints embedded within the document structure.
sections.plainLanguage: Old documents and scholarly texts can have copyright, legal, or confidentiality rules. TEI lets people mark different parts with different ownership, and programs have to respect those rules.
